Rootless podman storage under `~/.local/share/containers` reached 412 GiB and was the second largest
consumer on a filesystem that had reached 96 percent used. `podman system df` reported 372.3 GB of
images with 369.2 GB, or 99 percent, reclaimable, which is the signature of images that test suites
build and never remove.

## Evidence

```text
TYPE           TOTAL       ACTIVE      SIZE        RECLAIMABLE
Images         5076        69          372.3GB     369.2GB (99%)
Containers     83          1           15.11GB     8.773GB (58%)
Local Volumes  12          4           5.67GB      5.496GB (97%)
```

5037 images were in the rootless store. 467 were dangling with repository `<none>`, and 310 were
tagged `localhost/*`, meaning they were built locally rather than pulled. The largest groups by
repository:

```text
 78  localhost/git-policy-native-test
 60  localhost/git-policy-native-mutation
 13  localhost/monochromatic-lint-test
 11  localhost/mutation-test-runtime
 10  localhost/scanner-clippy
 10  localhost/monochromatic-lint-mutation
  8  localhost/scanner-test
  7  localhost/git-policy-cli-fuzz-run
  7  localhost/git-policy-cli-fuzz-build
  4  localhost/cli-git-concurrent-e2e-native
  3  localhost/scanner-guard-protected
  3  localhost/scanner-embedding-fuzz
  3  localhost/monochromatic-lint-fuzz-run
  3  localhost/monochromatic-lint-fuzz-build
  3  localhost/git-policy-native-interop
```

Counts of 78 and 60 for two repositories indicate repeated rebuilds under the same tag, each
leaving the previous image dangling. That accounts for most of the 467 `<none>` entries.

The 12 volumes were all development caches rather than user data, named `nested-wayland-session-cargo`,
`terminal-cargo`, `pnpr-prototype-cargo-registry`, `pnpr-prototype-rustup`, `ide-cargo`,
`ide-lsp-spike-cargo`, `music-player-cargo`, and five hash-named entries.

## Why this is not just a prune problem

`podman image prune --all --force` exited 125 with seven `image is in use by a container: consider
listing external containers and force-removing image` errors, so a plain prune does not fully
reclaim even when it is run. The remedy is `--external`. Running `container prune` first does not
help, because external containers live only in containers/storage and are invisible to podman's
own prune. Details and source citations are in
`doc/troubleshooting/podman-image-prune-external-containers.md`.

Because these steps were chained with `&&`, the image prune failure also skipped a trailing
`volume prune`, so the 5.496 GiB of reclaimable volume space was silently left behind.

## Impact

On btrfs the cost exceeds the raw size, because snapper's hourly snapshots of `/var/home` pin the
blocks of every deleted image until each referencing snapshot is also removed. See
`doc/troubleshooting/snapper-space-limits-not-enforced.md`.

## Suggested direction

Suites that build images should remove them on teardown, or reuse a stable tag with `--layers` so
rebuilds share history instead of each leaving a dangling parent. A periodic repo task that reports
`localhost/*` image count and total reclaimable size would make recurrence visible before it
reaches hundreds of gigabytes.

## Context

The oxlint feature-parity work on `package/linter/rust` needs a config file.
TOML was chosen for the first pass because the Rust binary can read it natively
with no external runtime, keeping `rust-linter` a standalone binary.

Pkl was the preferred format during the design discussion but was set aside,
so this issue records the alternatives and the facts each one turns on.

Design context: `doc/planning/rust-linter-oxlint-parity.md`, decision D3.

## Why TOML was not obviously right

- oxlint's own config is JSON/JSONC with a published
  `configuration_schema.json` (`node_modules/oxlint/configuration_schema.json`).
  TOML means hand-designing a mapping of the same concepts
  (`rules`, `categories`, `overrides`, `extends`, `ignorePatterns`, `options`)
  into TOML's array-of-tables shape, so the two linters' configs diverge and
  oxlint's schema is not reusable for editor completion.
- The config also carries the declarative pattern-rule language chosen in
  decision D4, so config expressiveness is load-bearing, not cosmetic.
- TOML has no types, no validation, and no composition, so shared rule sets
  across the repo's 15 Rust packages get duplicated rather than derived,
  which is exactly what `package/config/oxlint/src/overrides.ts` exists to
  avoid on the TypeScript side.

## Alternatives to evaluate

### Pkl

Typed, validated, composable, and the format originally preferred.

Blockers found during the design discussion, both of which need re-checking
before adopting:

- The repo deliberately retired Pkl in #357
  ("build(cli-git): retire hk and Pkl after policy parity"), removing root
  `hk.pkl`, the `apple/pkl` mise tool declaration, and `.idea/pklSettings.xml`.
  Adopting Pkl re-adds that tool.
- Rust cannot embed a Pkl evaluator. `rpkl` (0.8.0, June 2026, 34 percent doc
  coverage) works by spawning `pkl server` and exchanging MessagePack over
  stdio. Pkl native binaries cover macOS amd64/aarch64, Linux amd64/aarch64,
  Alpine amd64, and Windows amd64.

So Pkl means choosing one of: `pkl eval` into a generated JSON artifact at
build time, a hybrid where the binary reads generated JSON but accepts `.pkl`
via `--config`, or a runtime dependency on the `pkl` executable for every
invocation.

### JSONC

Literal oxlint parity: the same shape, the same `$schema` editor integration,
no build step. Costs the composition that `overrides.ts` provides today, and
makes pattern rules painful because every backslash and newline needs escaping.

### TypeScript, rendered to a machine-readable artifact

Matches `AGENTS.md` AD2 and the existing `oxlint.config.ts` authoring style,
but a Rust binary cannot execute TypeScript, so it needs a generated artifact
and a file-enforcer entry, the same shape as the Pkl build-time option.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Re-evaluate Pkl, JSONC, and TypeScript-rendered config against the
      TOML config as it actually stands once oxlint parity has landed,
      including how well each expresses the pattern-rule language.
- [ ] Decide whether the binary may acquire a build-time config artifact,
      and if so whether file-enforcer owns it.
- [ ] Record the outcome in `doc/decision/`, superseding decision D3 in
      `doc/planning/rust-linter-oxlint-parity.md`.
result.title: Revisit rust-linter config format after oxlint parity lands (Pkl, JSONC, or rendered TypeScript)

(`doc/planning/monorepo-manager-route-research/mise-task-usage.md`).

`mise.toml:681-698` spawns only the root `test:unit`,

and `test:e2e` suites.
Root `test:unit` globs `**/*.unit.test.ts`.

23 package-level `test` tasks exist,

which that glob cannot reach.
So those packages' tests never run from the root.

`//:lint` does fan out,
through `{{vars.fanout_packages}}`,
so lint reaches these packages while test does not.
`//:validate` and `//:buildAndTest` inherit the gap.

Fixing it means deciding whether root `test` should fan out the way `lint` does.

`mise.toml:308-312` justifies 85 lines of hand-written cross-package orchestration by saying the native

## What happened

`@monochromatic-dev/module-translation-repair` began importing
`@monochromatic-dev/cli-markdown-lint`, to run the `semantic-line-breaks` fix over text
the pipeline ships. After that, **every import of the translation-repair package threw
before reaching a line of pipeline code**:

```text
Cannot find native binding. npm has a bug related to optional dependencies
(https://github.com/npm/cli/issues/4828). Please try `npm i` again after
removing both package-lock.json and node_modules directory.
```

The message names npm and optional dependencies. Both are red herrings, and the message
is emitted by Sätteri's napi loader, not by npm or pnpm.

## What is actually going on

Sätteri is a napi package. Its loader calls `require("@bruits/satteri-<platform>")` and
resolves that relative to wherever the loader's own file sits.

The shared rolldown Node config always bundles `@monochromatic-dev/**` and keeps only
DECLARED dependencies external
(`package/config/rolldown/src/index.node.ts`, `package/config/rolldown/README.md`).
So importing the markdown-lint workspace package inlined its source, its `satteri`
import, and Sätteri's loader, into
`package/module/translation-repair/dist/final/node/`.

That directory is not Sätteri's package directory. Resolution from there walks up and
finds no `@bruits/*` link, because pnpm links those under Sätteri's own location and
nowhere else.

## What it is NOT, with the checks that rule each out

**The bindings are installed.** `node_modules/.pnpm` carries
`@bruits+satteri-linux-x64-gnu@0.9.5` and its siblings for every architecture in
`supportedArchitectures`.

**Sätteri resolves them correctly from its own location.** Two independent checks:
`node package/cli/markdown-lint/dist/final/node/cli.mjs <file>` lints and exits 0, and a
scratch script importing markdown-lint's own `dist` ran the fixer over 64 passages with
no binding error.

**`packageExtensions` does not apply.** It adds dependencies to another package's
manifest so pnpm links them under it, curing the case where a package imports something
it never declared, which under this workspace's strict isolation
(`hoist: false`, `nodeLinker: isolated`) is unresolvable FROM THAT PACKAGE'S OWN
LOCATION. `pnpm-workspace.yaml` carries exactly one such entry, `mitata` reaching for
`@mitata/counters`, and its comment states that shape precisely. This failure has the
opposite shape: nothing is missing from Sätteri's location, the code was copied OUT of
that location by the bundler. Editing Sätteri's manifest changes what pnpm links under
Sätteri, which the inlined copy in `dist/final/node/` never consults.

## Current workaround, which is why this issue exists rather than a closed bug

Declaring the transitive dependency in the consumer:

```jsonc
// package/module/translation-repair/package.json
"satteri": "catalog:",
```

Declared means external, so the bundle emits a runtime import rather than a copy, and
node resolves it from the consuming package's own `node_modules`, where Sätteri sits
beside the `@bruits/*` links its loader needs. Verified by reading the built bundle:

```text
grep 'from"satteri"'                    1 match
grep 'Cannot find native binding'       0 files
grep '@bruits/satteri-[a-z0-9-]*'       0 matches
```

**This works and it is a trap.** Any package that imports markdown-lint must declare a
native dependency it never mentions in its own source, learned only by hitting the
failure. The failure surfaces at import time rather than at build time, so a green build
says nothing about it, and the error text points at npm.

## What this issue asks for

1. **Write the troubleshooting doc for the setup as it stands**, so the next person to
   import markdown-lint recognises the error instead of chasing npm and
   `packageExtensions`. It needs the symptom verbatim, the bundling cause, the three
   negative checks above, and the bundle-reading verification.

2. **Then resolve it properly by migrating to an alternative setup**, so the workaround
   stops being load-bearing.

## Candidate alternatives

Relevant history: `doc/handover/markdown-lint-satteri-benchmark.md` records that Sätteri
was adopted as a PARSER SWAP (variant 2) for speed, replacing
`mdast-util-from-markdown` plus micromark, and that the rule engine kept consuming a
standard `mdast.Root`. The rules are therefore already parser-agnostic, which is what
makes the first option cheap.

**A. Split markdown-lint so the rule core carries no parser.** A core package exporting
rules and a fix driver over an `mdast.Root`, with Sätteri confined to the CLI that reads
files.
Pros: consumers importing rules never touch native code, so the trap disappears at its
source rather than being documented; the CLI keeps the measured speed; matches the
parser-agnostic shape the rules already have.
Cons: a new package and a moved subpath; every consumer of `parse` has to say which
parser it wants; `doc/troubleshooting/satteri-offsets.md` records that Sätteri and
micromark offsets differ, so a core used with either parser needs that pinned by a test.

**B. Carve `@monochromatic-dev/cli-markdown-lint` out of `NODE_ALWAYS_BUNDLE`.**
Pros: smallest change, one list entry; fixes every future consumer at once.
Cons: contradicts the deliberate reason `dist/final/node` exists, recorded in
`package/module/translation-repair/rolldown.node.config.ts`, that the executed thing
should be a FILE rather than an import graph; and it treats one package as special
without a rule saying which others are.

**C. Teach the rolldown config to keep any napi package external automatically**, by
detecting `.node` loaders or an `optionalDependencies` binding set in the closure of
what it is about to bundle.
Pros: cures the class rather than this instance, and needs no consumer to know anything.
Cons: the detection is a heuristic on other people's package shapes, and a wrong answer
either re-breaks the bundle or silently externalises something that should be inlined.

**D. Keep the declaration and document it.**
Pros: nothing to build.
Cons: this is the status quo the issue is filed against.

Ranking: A > C > B > D.

A over C because A removes the native dependency from the consumer's path entirely,
while C only stops it being copied: with C, a consumer still ships a runtime dependency
on a native package it never asked for, and the install has to keep working everywhere
that consumer runs.
C over B because C states a rule the build applies to every package, where B names one
package as special and leaves the next napi dependency to fail the same way.
B over D because B at least makes the failure impossible rather than merely legible.

## Reproduction

```bash
git revert --no-commit <the commit adding "satteri": "catalog:">
mise run //package/module/translation-repair:build
node -e 'import("./package/module/translation-repair/dist/final/node/index.mjs")'
```

Argument scanning (C577, C698, C902). `isOptionToken` (`src/parser/argv.ts:157-160`, using `LONE_DASH`) and `isOption` (`src/index-lock/index-writer-commands.ts:123-125`, using a literal `'-'`) state the same rule. `optionRegion` is character-identical in four parser modules (`add.ts:87-100`, `clean.ts:107-120`, `reset.ts:92-105`, `stash.ts:64-77`). The Rust side duplicates the wrapper-flag scan between `src/native/command_config.rs:178-190` and `src/native/command_stash.rs:209-222`. Policy results and events (C289, C867, C789, C895). The blocking-event predicate exists in the engine (`src/policy-engine/engine.ts:399-402`) and again in its own e2e fixture (`e2e/jsonl-event-fixture.ts:216-218`). Two failure-result builders (`src/policy-engine/commit-transaction-results.ts:36-63` and `:85-112`) restate the same exit code 2, `shouldForward: false` and failure-event shape. Two staged-delta comparisons differ in null tolerance (`add-staged-delta.ts:194-196` versus `commit-capture-order-capture.ts:189-191`, where absent maps compare equal and report no change). Two user-facing messages for an unselected fix path share a verbatim `git restore --staged --worktree -- ` remediation sentence (`src/policy-engine/commit-transaction-added-paths.ts:94-99` and `:100-105`). **Desired behavior:** A small set of shared modules inside `git-policy/cli`: - one patch builder owning the header, the mode selection, the line splitter and the no-newline marker, used by the markdown-lint package and the policy engine; - one byte-order comparator with the encoding stated once (git orders by raw bytes, which for UTF-8 paths means `utf8`); - one path-safety module (traversal segments including the empty case, absolute-path resolution with an explicit base, containment); - one process-liveness probe with a stated `EPERM` policy; - one git invocation helper (spawn, cwd, pre-subcommand args, trim policy, subprocess-error classification); - one object-bytes resolver covering the submodule case and the missing-blob error; - one argument-scanning module shared by the TypeScript parsers and one wrapper-flag scan shared by the two Rust command parsers; - one failure-result builder and one blocking-event predicate imported by the e2e fixture. Cons: a wide change across the policy engine, the parser, the native crate and the e2e fixtures; needs the e2e suite green at each step. 2. **Fix the four divergences and share only the helpers they need.** The encoding disagreement, the empty-segment gap, the `EPERM` policy and the no-newline marker are the four that can produce a wrong result today; sharing the byte-order comparator, the segment predicate, the liveness probe and the patch builder fixes them and leaves the rest. Pros: smallest change that removes every correctness risk named here. Cons: the remaining copies can drift the same way later. 3. **Fix the divergences in place, share nothing.** Pros: no structural change. Cons: five byte-order comparators and two patch builders stay, so the next change repeats the problem. **Ranking:** 2 > 1 > 3. Option 2 ranks above 1 because the four divergences are defects with user-visible consequences (a wrong ordering for non-ASCII paths, an accepted `..`-free but empty segment, an exception where a lock check would report alive, a patch marker `git apply` may reject) and fixing them does not require migrating every helper. result.body:
`openSemanticFile` keeps the text it was handed for every source, and reports a deletion only for
the immediately previous active source:

```ts
const deletedFiles = (bridgeState.activeFileName !== NO_ACTIVE_FILE)
  && (bridgeState.activeFileName !== normalizedFileName)
  && (!existsSync(bridgeState.activeFileName,))
  ? [bridgeState.activeFileName,]
  : [];
```

Those two facts do not compose. Lint `a.ts`, then `b.ts`, then `c.ts`, and delete `a.ts` from disk.
Nothing ever reports `a.ts` as deleted, because it stopped being the active source before it was
removed. Its overlay entry survives, so `fileExists` keeps answering true for it and `readFile`
keeps returning the text it held, and the native service goes on resolving that source as present
with content that no longer exists anywhere.

## Impact

Under Oxlint this is largely unreachable: sources exist while a sweep reads them, and a sweep is
shorter than the lifetime of a deletion. It is reachable for any longer-lived host, an editor
integration or a watch mode, which is the same class of caller the retained overlays were introduced
to serve.

## Why it is not a one-line fix

The cheap spelling, checking every retained overlay for existence on every open, is a syscall per
retained source per lint, which is the cost the directory memo in `cachedProjectForFile` was
introduced to avoid. Plausible directions, none obviously right:

- Check existence only for overlays whose directory changed since the last open.
- Give overlays an eviction bound and report eviction as deletion.
- Have the caller drive deletion, since a host that deletes a file knows it did.

## Origin

Found by review of the announcement classification fixed in #439 and #440, alongside the failed
discovery staleness fixed in 58664cb1e. Same family: bridge state describing a service that has
moved on. This one is unlikely enough under the current caller that it should not be fixed by
guessing at the strategy.

## Goal

Full-repository warm oxlint under 60 seconds wall time.

## Current state (2026-07-15, after the traversal-narrowing refactor)

- Serial whole-repo sweep `mise run lint:oxlint`:
  1,639 s warm (2,561 files, one single-threaded instance).
  Pre-refactor baseline was 816.5 s
  (`docs/planning/replace-prefer-readonly-parameter-types.md`,
  final verification record);
  live workspace-source analysis roughly doubled the serial scope.
- New parallel task `mise run lint:oxlint:fanout`
  (commit `cd812155a`):
  fans out per-package `lint:oxlint` through the bounded worker pool,
  one single-threaded instance each,
  then lints root-level files the package scopes never reach.
  Best measured wall time: 85 s warm
  (5.5 CPU-minutes across the pool),
  a 19x improvement over the serial sweep,
  but still above the 60 s goal.

## Remaining work

1. Parallel reliability:
   each fanout run so far had a few children die with
   "Command failed: oxlint-wrapper" and no lint output;
   every such child passes serially afterward.
   First run also raced concurrent `build:js:node` of shared config
   dependencies (separate `mise run` processes do not dedupe depends).
   Suspects: persistent effect-summary cache write contention and
   memory pressure from ~parallelism semantic bridges.
   The old migration record mentions "lock and cache race fixes";
   verify they cover cross-process fanout.
2. Warm cache payoff diagnosis:
   the serial sweep's second (warm) run took 1,639 s versus 1,552 s cold,
   so the persistent/final-index caches do not pay off at whole-repo scope;
   find out why (cache identity churn per active file? verify-phase
   RPC cost dominating?).
3. Per-package debt keeping children red:
   `dev-script/deps-cube` has 11 pre-existing warnings
   (no-unsafe-assignment, chain-per-line) unrelated to the readonly rule.
4. Root-scope debt:
   root-level files outside package scopes carry ~240 warnings / ~203
   errors of accepted pre-existing debt
   (recorded baseline: 3,792 / 665 whole-repo),
   which keeps any whole-repo aggregate red until that backlog is swept.
5. If parallelism plus cache fixes still miss 60 s:
   the summary-artifact fallback design
   (per-package effect summaries emitted at build time)
   is the named escalation in
   `docs/planning/prefer-readonly-traversal-narrowing.md`.

## Constraint

Each oxlint/tsc instance must stay single-threaded
(semantic bridge state is process-local);
parallelism comes from running many instances.

**Summary:** 22 clusters in the current duplicate-code report were reviewed for dismissal. 13 are proposed for `slopo.ignore.txt`; 9 are held back. The 9 held entries are there 9 because the pattern behind them propagates and needs an owner (a utility, base class or macro) that does not exist yet or does not know about them. The test is propagation rather than size: a pattern instantiated twice is a template for the third copy, so "too small to extract" is not a sufficient reason to dismiss. The classification of all 86 concepts behind the four dismissal issues, and the measurements behind it, are in `doc/planning/slopo-dismissed-cluster-actionability.md`. This issue proposes entries; it does not change any source file.

**Current behavior:**

Current state: all 22 clusters appear in every report generated from the 2026-10-07 index and none is in `slopo.ignore.txt`, so each costs a reviewer's attention on every run.

Each cluster's reported bodies were read individually and the review ledger records what the two sides do. The recorded verification mode is `full-read` (reported bodies read in full) for all 22, not `file-inspected`, so callers, ownership and existing utilities were not examined; that is the confidence level these verdicts carry. The pairs:

- **Different destination grammars** (C187 `modulePath` strips at the first `?` while `stripAttrQuery` strips only at the import-attributes query; C588 and C599 shell single-quote escaping versus git-config double-quote escaping; C706 three git wire-format line builders for the index record, batch-ref-update create line and packed-refs line). Merging any of these as written would change behaviour for one side. Caveat 3 states what that does and does not prove: `SYB` requires encoding at the final interpolation for the destination grammar, which a parameterised encoder could satisfy, so the reason these stay separate is that a shared version would carry no policy, not that the grammar forbids it.
- **Different domains that share a shape** (C315 comparators over file/line/name versus start/end/text, C358 three two-key comparators where one is descending for mutation safety, C363 two key-allowlist filters with unrelated key sets, C837 two image-diff CLI formatters projecting different result fields, C342 three one-line string formatters for trust evidence and fuzz sample output, C811 `toSummary` and `toMinimal` projections, C909 two retirement key builders for family versus exact identity, C937 `isSafeHtml` and `isDangerousHtml` guards for two html-carrying conventions, C575 an LRU entry generator and a config-store iterator, C833 two path-segment helpers where one resolves first).

C293, two offset-carrying Rust `Display` impls, was described here in the first version of this issue but is not proposed by it: its recorded verdict is `BOILERPLATE-TRIVIAL`, #656 owns it, and its shared JSONC dependency is a fact about extraction, not a reason to dismiss.

Add the 13 proposed hashes listed at the end of this issue to `slopo.ignore.txt`, each under the heading its recorded verdict names and each keeping the complete comment proposed there. The 9 held-back entries are listed beside them with the owner or decision each waits on, and their hashes are not proposed for the file.

Each entry states what the two sides do, so a future reviewer can disagree with a specific reason rather than re-deriving the comparison. The cost of being wrong is bounded: deleting the hash line restores visibility, and no runtime behaviour depends on the file. The cost of the opposite choice is reviewer attention on every run for a match nobody will act on.

## Context

`packages/kwin/key-helper` depends on `dbus-next@0.10.2`, last published 2022-04-28 and effectively unmaintained. It was the sole source of 14 Dependabot advisories, cleared in 516980e19 via two `pnpm.overrides` (drop the optional native `usocket`, floor `xml2js` to `>=0.5.0`). See the audit in `docs/troubleshooting/dependencies.md` (`### dbus-next`).

Those overrides stop the bleeding but leave the unmaintained library itself in the tree, including its deprecated direct dep `event-stream@3.3.4` (the package of the 2018 backdoor incident; this pinned version predates it, so no advisory, but it is dead weight and a latent supply-chain surface).

## Task

Retire `dbus-next` for a maintained D-Bus path. Candidates to evaluate (via the `choosing-technology` skill):

- `@httptoolkit/dbus-native`, an actively maintained fork of `dbus-native`.
- Shelling out to `busctl` / `gdbus` for the small surface key-helper uses.

## Scope notes

- key-helper is server-only: it answers `Introspect` via `xml2js`'s Builder and never parses XML (`src/sax-stub.ts`). Any replacement only needs to publish an interface, own a bus name, and emit signals, not parse introspection XML.
- It connects to the session bus over the systemd path socket and passes no file descriptors, so native FD-passing is not required.
- Re-test the daemon against a live KWin/Plasma session bus, since unit tests do not exercise the D-Bus path.

## Acceptance

- `dbus-next`, `event-stream`, and the two `dbus-next>*` overrides are gone from `pnpm-workspace.yaml` / `pnpm-lock.yaml`.
- The daemon's active-window tracking, Ctrl+F4, Meta+N, and double-shift-to-F20 behaviours work against a real session bus.

## Summary

`packages/webapp-productivity/done` runs a migration that creates an FTS5 virtual table.
When the `@tursodatabase/database` native build in use does not include the FTS5 extension, migration fails and the app cannot start.

## Where

`packages/webapp-productivity/done/src/lib/db-migrations.ts` (`MIGRATION_FTS_AND_TRIGGERS`):

```sql
CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE IF NOT EXISTS tasks_fts USING fts5(
  title,
  description,
  tags,
  content=tasks,
  content_rowid=rowid
);
```

Plus the `tasks_fts_insert` / `tasks_fts_update` triggers that keep the index in sync.
This runs via `await db.exec(...)` inside `runMigrations`, which `src/lib/db.ts` imports for its side effects on startup.

## Symptom

Any path that triggers migrations (starting the server, opening the database) fails at the FTS5 `CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE` when the loaded turso build lacks the `fts5` module.
Observed in a container where the `@tursodatabase/database` prebuilt native binary does not include FTS5; the failure occurs before any application query runs.

`done` pins turso through the workspace catalog:

```jsonc
// packages/webapp-productivity/done/package.json
"@tursodatabase/database": "catalog:"
```

## Options

- Ensure the pinned `@tursodatabase/database` build ships with FTS5 (select a build or feature flag that includes it), and document the requirement.
- Or make the full-text index optional: guard the FTS migration and the search path so `done` degrades to non-FTS search when FTS5 is unavailable.

## Notes

`done`'s `lint` passes; this is a runtime/migration defect, surfaced while remediating oxlint findings in the package. The lint fixes are unrelated to this defect.

## What to build

Harden the automatic patch transaction from #351 across the complete supported Git commit surface and make the ref-update/index-install gap recoverable after process interruption. Unsupported interactive modes remain read-only and block only when a fix is required.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Amend, allow-empty, pathspec files, deletion, selected untracked paths, merge/cherry-pick/revert conclusions, and clean/unmerged index states have explicit supported/rejected semantics and fixtures.
- [ ] Merge/cherry-pick/revert conclusions use index-commit semantics and never emulate partial explicit-path conclusions.
- [ ] A durable journal records original HEAD/index identity, prepared post-index, and intended result before real Git can advance a ref.
- [ ] Recovery distinguishes commit-not-created, commit-created-before-index-install, completed install, stale journal, and conflicting external movement without discarding user state.
- [ ] The real index lock prevents concurrent index mutation for the transaction and every lock/journal/temp artifact has interruption cleanup coverage.
- [ ] The complete policy sequence has an eight-pass cap, exact path-and-byte stability comparison, non-adjacent cycle detection, provisional changed-pass findings, and immediate engine-failure stop.
- [ ] Temporary pass states use private storage and streaming exact comparisons rather than cli-git content hashes or duplicate in-memory snapshots.
- [ ] Interactive/patch/include modes proceed when already canonical and block with direct-fix guidance only when a patch is required.
- [ ] Adversarial fixtures cover hook failure, patch traversal/unexpected path, rename/mode/submodule operations, binary patches, signals, filesystem errors, and recovery on the next shim invocation.

- #351

Measured on `translation-repair-rebased` after merging `main` (merge commit `336b1673e`), package `@monochromatic-dev/module-translation-repair`, via `mise run //package/module/translation-repair:lint:oxlint`.

The merge did improve the rule: five findings from other rules surfaced and were fixed, and one prefer-readonly finding became reachable by an ordinary rewrite. What remains is 118 findings, and a subset of them cannot be resolved by any change to this package.

## The blocking class: the rule offers an outcome the toolchain forbids

47 of the 118 findings carry this paragraph verbatim:

```text
This input is already readonly at every level, so no type change resolves this finding. A readonly type is
erased at compile time: the call still receives the underlying object and this rule cannot see whether it
writes to it.

Resolve it by one of these changes, or accept it:
1. Include the exact repository-owned implementation in the nearest tsconfig.json so the rule can inspect it.
2. Pass a copy the callee may keep, so no caller-owned identity crosses the boundary.
3. Remove or replace the call so no caller-owned input reaches unresolved code.
```

"or accept it" is not expressible. The finding is reported at severity `error`, and
`package/config/oxlint/src/rule/restriction.ts:198` sets
`no-restricted-syntax/no-disable-prefer-readonly-parameter-types` to `error`, so a scoped disable comment
fails too. There is no annotation, config key, or contract that records an accepted finding, which means a
package holding one of these can never pass `lint`.

The three listed resolutions do not reach this class either. The unresolved callees are ECMAScript
built-ins, so option 1 has no repository-owned implementation to include; option 2 asks for a deep copy at
every boundary that touches a collection; option 3 asks for the call not to happen.

Example, `src/repair-region.ts` before the rewrite below: `collectRepairRegions` takes
`readonly envelopes: readonly EditableEnvelope[]` and `readonly applied: readonly PatchOperation[]`,
mutates nothing, and returns fresh objects. It was reported for "a call whose name this rule could not
determine", which was `new Map(...)` plus `Map.get`.

## What a consumer can and cannot reach

Fixable, and done: replacing `new Map` plus `Map.get` with record indexing cleared that finding and took
the package from 119 to 118. `applied.map(...)` was left in place and the rule accepts it, so callbacks that
are owned source are not the problem.

That fix has a cost worth naming: it traded an immutable `new Map(...)` construction for a record built by a
`for...of` loop, which is contrary to `AGENTS.md` `IMM` (prefer immutable patterns and functional approaches
over mutable state and imperative loops). `LN1` forbids satisfying one rule by violating another, and here
the two pull opposite ways. Every functional alternative for building a lookup is opaque as well:
`Map` construction and `get`, `Object.fromEntries`, `reduce` with a seed, `Array.find`. So the only shapes
this rule accepts for an index are the ones `IMM` steers away from.

Not fixable in this package, 14 findings:

```text
src/front-matter.ts:79        super           (native Error constructor)
src/corpus-source.ts:105      super
src/synthetic-quota.ts:91     super
src/parse-mdx.ts:36           super
src/completion-shape.ts:99    super
src/stream-drain.ts:72        response.text, body.getReader
src/synthetic-transport.ts:109 AbortSignal.any, fetch
src/call-deadline.ts:52       signal.addEventListener, signal.removeEventListener, callController.abort
src/synthetic-client.ts:173   JSON.stringify, signal.addEventListener, signal.removeEventListener, abort
src/synthetic-client.ts:288   JSON.stringify, signal.addEventListener, signal.removeEventListener, abort
src/repair-translation.ts:188 JSON.stringify, reduce, map, get
src/repair-benchmark.ts:424   JSON.stringify, reduce, map, get
src/recall-benchmark.ts:137   sizer.encode   (TextEncoder)
src/grade-agreement.ts:171    String
```

These carry a fourth option, marking the input `ForeignHostCapability` with an `@mutates` contract. That
path is right for the genuinely host-owned ones (`Response`, `AbortSignal`), and `stream-drain.ts` should
probably be corrected from `ForeignBorrowed<Response>` to `ForeignHostCapability<Response>` regardless. It
is wrong for the rest: `AGENTS.md` `JCH` forbids `@mutates` for absent effects, and a `cause: unknown`
handed to `super`, a `JSON.stringify` of caller data, and `TextEncoder.encode` are not host capabilities
that mutate their argument. Writing a contract to silence the analyzer is exactly what `JCH` names as the
failure.

## Remaining classes, for scale

```text
 47  already readonly at every level, no type change applies
 34  collection calls with a functional alternative (push, set, get, toSorted, reduce, flat, values)
 29  filter, flatMap, map where the closure hands back captured state
 14  host boundaries and super, listed above
 11  a call whose name the rule could not determine
```

The 29 have a documented recovery path in `doc/troubleshooting/oxlint-prefer-readonly-retained-closure.md`
and were not attempted here; the guide's own last entry for them is "accept the withholding", which runs
into the same expressibility problem as the 47.

## What would unblock this package

Ranked, with the reason each beats the next.

1. Make the "already readonly at every level" case a warning rather than an error. It beats the others
   because the rule's own diagnostic already concludes no type change resolves it, so an error asserts a
   defect the rule says cannot be repaired.
2. Give acceptance an expression: a TSDoc tag or config key that records a reviewed opaque call, which
   `no-disable-prefer-readonly-parameter-types` would then not have to forbid. Weaker than 1 only because
   it adds surface that has to be reviewed.
3. Add an override for packages that cross host boundaries, as
   `package/config/oxlint/src/overrides.ts` already does for the rule's own package under the self-hosting
   boundary. Ranked last because it turns the rule off wholesale and loses the findings that are real.

Not proposed: loosening the rule globally, or writing `@mutates` contracts for effects that do not happen.

## What to build

Add trusted TypeScript config authoring on top of stored-snapshot trust. When MJS is absent, `git cli-git trust` builds repo-root TypeScript through tsdown into one immutable Node ESM bundle, records exact entry/relative-module snapshots, and executes only the stored bundle.

Strict mode compares exact bytes. Explicit per-path relaxed mode may rebuild automatically from source metadata without re-consent.

- [ ] MJS retains precedence when both config formats exist.
- [ ] The public tsdown `build()` API runs with config-file discovery disabled, Node ESM output, all packages forced into the bundle, and inline dynamic imports.
- [ ] Trust accepts exactly one JavaScript chunk with no unresolved non-Node imports or extra assets; failed/incomplete builds abort before persistent trust.
- [ ] Entry and statically resolved relative local modules are exact-snapshot invalidation inputs; lockfiles and bare package/workspace imports are not.
- [ ] Trust warns when source uses bare packages outside automatic invalidation even though current package code is bundled.

- [ ] `CLI_GIT_NO_PARANOID` uses the settled comma/percent exact-path grammar; malformed or planted entries emit a prominent warning, are ignored, retain strict behavior for that path, and never waive first trust.
- [ ] For a previously trusted relaxed path, tracked source mtime/size changes trigger automatic rebuild; rebuild failure blocks with exit `2`.

## Status

Plan drafted and posted: https://github.com/Aquaticat/Monochromatic/issues/247#issuecomment-4887670850 (scope grew beyond the body below: ground-up rewrite as packages/cli/mutation-test with sharded disposable containers; the plan comment supersedes the rough shape here). Implementation in progress.

## Motivation

Own the mutation tester the same way `@monochromatic-dev/module-test` replaced Vitest, and shed the StrykerJS + Babel dependency footprint entirely.

This is not about `convert-source-map`. That transitive edge is already neutralized and inert: Stryker's instrumenter is parse-only and never enters Babel's `transform` pipeline (the only place `@babel/core` requires `convert-source-map`), so the throwing stub is never loaded at runtime. See `docs/troubleshooting/dependencies.md` (the `convert-source-map` deep-dive) and `docs/troubleshooting/stryker-container-runtime.md`. The driver here is footprint and control, not a runtime bug.

## Goal

A container-native mutation testing framework, built on oxc, that replaces the Stryker-spawn core of `@monochromatic-dev/dev-script-mutation-test`, reusing that package's existing orchestration.

Container-native means the engine is designed to run inside the existing per-source Podman container (worktree, isolation, resource caps, no network), not as a host tool wrapped to look containerized. It integrates with the current container worktree, source/test selection, and JSON reporting rather than assuming a host runtime.

No Babel. The whole `@babel` subtree goes away; oxc owns parsing.

## Rough shape (to be designed, not prescriptive)

- Parse with oxc (`oxc-parser`). Locate mutable nodes by their source spans and apply each mutation by splicing replacement text at the node's byte offsets, which avoids a separate code-generation step entirely. Fall back to oxc transform/codegen only if span-splicing proves insufficient for some operator.
- Mutation operators reimplemented against oxc's ESTree-style AST, covering the same families as the ~15 Stryker mutators (arithmetic, equality, logical, conditional, boolean, string, unary, update, array, object, optional chaining, block statement, method expression, arrow function, regex).
- Per-mutant generate-and-run against `module-test` with kill detection (killed / survived / timeout / error), instead of mutation-switching.
- Optional TypeScript type-check filter to drop non-compiling mutants (Stryker's typescript-checker value-add). This is the hardest, riskiest piece and needs incremental tsc for acceptable speed.
- Reuse the existing container isolation, source/test selection, and report aggregation in `packages/dev-script/mutation-test/src` as-is.

## Measured baselines

- `packages/dev-script/mutation-test/src`: 3,516 code lines; only 218 are Stryker-spawn glue (`stryker-config.ts`, `container-stryker.ts`, `inline-nu.ts`). The other ~3,300 (container, selection, reporting, CLI, runtime image) is reusable.
- `packages/module/test/src` precedent: 2,829 code lines.
- `@stryker-mutator/instrumenter` (engine to reimplement, complexity proxy only; we port operator logic, not Babel-specific code): 2,447 compiled lines (mutators 566, mutant-placers 215, transformers 374, parsers 422, util 341, top-level 307, printers 71, frameworks 88).
- Footprint dropped: 5 `@stryker-mutator` packages and the entire `@babel` subtree (~44 packages). oxc replaces parsing; span-splicing removes the need for a JS code generator.

## LoC estimate (engineering estimate, not measured)

- Minimum viable, no type-check filter: ~1,100 production + ~700 test new code lines; net production delta ~+900 after deleting the 218 glue lines. (oxc span-splicing keeps the parse/codegen glue small, since no generator is written.)
- Feature parity, with type-check filter: ~1,500 production + ~900 test new code lines.
- In raw file lines (TSDoc-everywhere house style, ~0.6 to 0.7 comments per code line): roughly 2,900 to 3,800 raw lines across new files.

## References

- `docs/troubleshooting/dependencies.md`
- `docs/troubleshooting/stryker-container-runtime.md`
- `packages/dev-script/mutation-test/`
- `packages/module/test/` (precedent)

## Context

file-enforcer's no-op run (every derived file already in sync) recomputes every derived output just to
content-diff it. There is no mtime or hash gate before the transform, so the recompute happens every
run and the content-diff is the only thing between "recomputed" and "written".

Full analysis, and the decision against a Rust rewrite, live in
`packages/dev-script/file-enforcer/DECISION.rust-migration.md` (commit f71b5b18).

Key facts from the trace:

-   `src/io/write.ts` `writeIfChanged` always computes the candidate content, reads the dest, and
    string-compares `existing === content`. It skips the write on equality, not the recompute.
-   `src/io/cache.ts` read cache is in-memory and per-process; a one-shot `mise run` starts cold.
-   `src/pipeline/exec.ts` subprocesses fire only on an action; a no-op run spawns none.
-   Existing mtime infrastructure: `src/watch/watch-filter.ts` stats files and compares `mtimeMs`
    against recorded write timestamps (`src/tracker.ts`), but only to classify our write echoes versus
    external edits, not to skip unchanged builders.

## Work

1.  Profile a real no-op run across the monorepo and confirm where time goes (predicted: file IO plus
    recompute, not parsing). Let the numbers gate the rest.
2.  Add a persisted staleness manifest: map each managed dest to a source-set hash (or mtime set) plus
    a dest hash; skip the transform, dest read, and compare when all match. This is the signal one-shot
    runs lack today, since `writeTimestamps` do not survive across process invocations.
3.  Extend watch mode to reuse the `watch-filter.ts` mtime signal as a build-skip gate, not only echo
    suppression.
4.  Optimize a specific parse-heavy builder only if the profile names one (for example, batch
    `parseTomlEdit` / `tomlSet` / `tomlStringify` in `src/pipeline/toml.ts` instead of re-parsing).

## Out of scope

Rust rewrite. Rejected in the decision doc: the builder API is consumed as TypeScript config modules
(`file-enforcer.config.ts` and per-package configs call `overwrite`, `cat`, `ensurePackage` with real
logic), which a native core cannot host.

## Acceptance

-   No-op run across the monorepo is measurably faster; record before and after numbers.
-   Correctness unchanged: a changed source still regenerates its dest, and an external edit to a
    managed dest is still detected and corrected.
-   `packages/test-fixture/file-enforcer-perf` exercises the no-op fast path under its throttled
    container constraints.

> *Original body was generated by AI during triage; corrected below where it was inaccurate or stale.*

## Intent

Publish `.pnpmfile.mjs` (the dependency blocklist hook) so other projects can consume it, ideally via pnpm's `configDependencies` mechanism.

## Background

pnpm 11 added [config dependencies](https://pnpm.io/config-dependencies). A published npm package whose name matches `pnpm-plugin-*`, `@*/pnpm-plugin-*`, or `@pnpm/plugin-*` is auto-loaded: pnpm reads `pnpmfile.mjs` from the package root, then runs the consumer's own pnpmfile on top.

Consumer declares it in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`:

\`\`\`yaml
configDependencies:
  '@monochromatic-dev/pnpm-plugin-dependency-blocklist': '^1.0.0'
\`\`\`

## What gets published

`.pnpmfile.mjs` lives at the repo root (the hook is ~194 lines since the policy table was split out to `.pnpmfile.policies.json`). Its `readPackage` hook walks every dependency field and rewrites blocklisted names to `workspace:@monochromatic-dev/stub-throwing@*` or `workspace:@monochromatic-dev/stub-silent@*`. The policy table covers Express 4.x abandoned utils, `caniuse-lite`, Babel polyfills, and the rest.

## Hard constraints from pnpm (corrected)

- The pnpmfile executes during resolution, before `node_modules` is populated, so the loaded file and anything it imports must rely on Node builtins only. The earlier claim that config dependencies cannot have their own dependencies overstated this: the binding constraint is the install-time bootstrap order plus registry and integrity resolution, not a blanket ban on declaring deps.
- A configDependency is resolved from the npm registry and integrity-pinned into an env-lockfile section of `pnpm-lock.yaml`; it cannot point at a `workspace:*` package, so we cannot dogfood our own unpublished package via configDependencies.
- The loaded pnpmfile must end in `.mjs`. `pnpmfileChecksum` hashes the loaded file's bytes only, not its imports, so edits to an imported helper or the policy JSON need `pnpm install --force`.

Full source citations against pnpm/pnpm HEAD are in the triage outcome comment.

## Open questions (status)

1. Package name. `@monochromatic-dev/pnpm-plugin-dependency-blocklist` for the configDependencies route; `@monochromatic-dev/config-pnpmfile` for the library-factory route.
2. Location. `packages/config/pnpmfile/` proposed.
3. Stub specifier rewrite. Still open: either rewrite to published version ranges (requires publishing the stubs first) or accept a stub-specifier override.
4. Policy customisation. Resolved in the drafted design: ship a generic factory `createReadPackageHook({ policies })` and keep the policy table repo-specific.
5. Versioning policy. Still open; document in the README when built.
6. Coordination with `pnpm-workspace.yaml` `overrides` companions. Still open; document the split for external consumers.
7. Testing without publishing. The library-factory route makes the factory unit-testable directly; the configDependencies route needs `npm pack` plus a tarball or file spec, since `workspace:*` is unavailable.

## References

- Source: `.pnpmfile.mjs`, `.pnpmfile.policies.json`
- Background: `docs/troubleshooting/pnpmfile.md`, `docs/dependency-blocklist.md`
- Upstream feature: <https://pnpm.io/config-dependencies>
- ESM hook loader PR: <https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/pull/9730>
- Related: #168 (upstream native-TS pnpmfile), #148 (refresh the blocklist)

## Agent brief

**Category:** enhancement
**State:** ready-for-agent
**Summary:** Re-implement runtime expression-position throwing in a dedicated `@monochromatic-dev/module-throws` package.

**Origin:** Extracted from #233. The classification decision is that `throws` should return, but not as a restored `module-es` root utility and not inside `module-or-throw`.

## Context

`module-es` still contains a historical stopgap at `packages/module/es/src/types/t never/f/t any/throws/r s/p n/index.ts`:

```ts
export function $({ value, }: { value: unknown; },): void {
  throw value;
}
```

That file says it exists until TC39 throw expressions become available. That future is not near enough to wait for: the TC39 proposal is still Stage 2, current Node and Bun reject the syntax, TypeScript is still waiting on TC39, and Oxc/Rolldown do not currently expose throw-expression parsing or lowering.

The current helper is also in the wrong home. `module-es` is being split and deleted. `module-or-throw` is not the right package either: its helpers assert that a value has a predicate shape and then return that same value. `throws` always throws and returns no value. It is a bottom helper, not an `*OrThrow` validator.

## Motivation

Existing `module-or-throw` helpers cover this shape:

```ts
const value = nonNullishOrThrow(maybeValue,);
```

They do not cover this shape without losing the domain error:

```ts
const value = maybeValue ?? throws(new MissingValueError(context,),);
```

The dedicated package keeps that rare expression-position need explicit and isolated. It also prevents broad utility creep in `module-or-throw` and avoids restoring `module-es` taxonomy APIs.

## Desired package

Create `packages/module/throws` with package name `@monochromatic-dev/module-throws`.

Initial public API:

```ts
/**
 * Throws an `Error` from expression position.
 *
 * @param error - Error instance to throw
 * @returns Never returns because it always throws
 * @throws Same `Error` instance passed by caller
 *
 * @example
 * ```ts
 * const token = maybeToken ?? throws(new MissingTokenError(),);
 * ```
 */
export function throws(error: Error,): never {
  throw error;
}
```

Use a direct named export from `src/index.ts`. Do not expose `$` from the old taxonomy path.

## Why `Error` input first

JavaScript permits throwing any value, but repo code should make the safe path easy:

- `Error` keeps stack, message, cause, and subclass identity available to catch sites.
- Passing a prebuilt `Error` lets the stack point at the call site in V8-style runtimes, instead of at the helper.
- Accepting `string` forces the helper to construct `new Error`, which moves stack capture into the helper.
- Accepting descriptor objects recreates the old `error.throws.ts` footgun: ad hoc mapping from `name` strings to constructors, no faithful custom subclass support, and extra policy in a primitive helper.
- Accepting `unknown` is closest to `throw` statement semantics, but it makes non-Error throws easy and makes catch-side handling worse.

If a real call site needs non-Error throws, open a follow-up issue or document the concrete use case in the PR before widening this API.

## Return type: `never` versus `void`

Use `never`.

`never` is the accurate type because control cannot continue past this function. It also preserves the main expression-position benefit:

```ts
const token: string = maybeToken ?? throws(new MissingTokenError(),);
```

With `never`, TypeScript sees the fallback branch as impossible to produce a value, so the result remains `string` when `maybeToken` is `string | undefined`.

`void` only says callers should ignore the returned value. It does not say the function cannot return. In expression position it pollutes fallback types with `void`, undermining the reason the helper exists. The existing module-es stopgap returning `void` is therefore a typing bug, not a model to preserve.

The only argument for `void` is that `throw` statements do not produce a value. That argument does not fit a helper whose whole purpose is to stand in for expression syntax. `never` communicates the runtime behavior and gives the type checker the needed control-flow fact.

## Footguns to avoid

- Do not add `string` overloads. They capture stacks inside the helper.
- Do not add descriptor-object overloads. They recreate custom error subclass ambiguity.
- Do not use `Error.captureStackTrace`. It is V8-specific and this repo targets Firefox ESR.
- Do not log the thrown error or its message. Error messages can include secrets and the caller owns logging policy.
- Do not advertise this as a replacement for statement `throw`. It is for rare expression-only slots.
- Do not encourage nested ternary control flow. Prefer statements or domain-specific `xOrThrow()` helpers when clearer.
- Do not place this in `module-or-throw`; that package returns validated values, while this package returns `never`.

## Implementation steps

1. Create `packages/module/throws` using sibling module package conventions.
2. Add `package.json`, `mise.toml`, `tsconfig.json`, and tsdown config mirroring focused module packages.
3. Implement `src/throws.ts` and re-export it from `src/index.ts`.
4. Add comprehensive TSDoc with expression-position examples and the `never` rationale.
5. Add unit tests through `@monochromatic-dev/module-test/ts`:
   - throws the exact same `Error` instance;
   - works in a `??` expression without widening the non-nullish branch;
   - return type is `never` via `expectTypeOf`;
   - no string or descriptor overload is exposed.
6. Add `README.md` documenting when to use this helper and when to prefer statements or `module-or-throw` validators.
7. Remove, deprecate, or retarget the old `module-es` stopgap so the focused package is the only intended home.
8. Update stale TODO or audit references that still mention the old helper returning `void`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `@monochromatic-dev/module-throws` exists under `packages/module/throws`.
- [ ] `throws(error: Error): never` is exported from the package root.
- [ ] The package has no runtime dependencies unless a PR explains why one is required.
- [ ] Unit tests cover runtime throwing, exact instance identity, expression typing, and `never` typing.
- [ ] README explains motivation, footguns, and relationship to `module-or-throw`.
- [ ] The old `module-es` stopgap no longer appears to be the supported public home.
- [ ] `mise run //packages/module/throws:lint` passes.
- [ ] `mise run //packages/module/throws:buildAndTest` passes.

## Context

The `find*Root` finders in `packages/module/fs-path` (`findMiseMonorepoRoot`, `findGitRepoRoot`,
`findPnpmWorkspaceRoot`, their `*Cached` variants, plus the sibling `find*PackageRoot` family)
have tests asserting that several values all resolve to one directory. Today that is written as a
transitive `toBe` chain:

```ts
expect(miseRoot,).toBe(gitRoot,);
expect(gitRoot,).toBe(pnpmRoot,);
```

This is correct (since `toBe` is `===` and `===` is transitive, the chain does prove all three equal)
but noisy to read and fiddly to extend: a reader must verify each line's right side is the next line's
left side, and adding a fourth value means remembering to link the chain rather than leaving a gap.

The ask: evaluate an "all equal" assertion for the harness and decide which flavor to adopt.

## Prevalence (measured)

Swept all 466 `*.test.ts` files for the transitive-chain shape. It appears in 3 files, concentrated in
the family named above:

- `packages/module/fs-path/src/find-monorepo-root.unit.test.ts` (heaviest; ~7 assertion clusters)
- `packages/module/fs-path/src/find-package-root.unit.test.ts`
- `packages/module/logger/src/sinks/file.unit.test.ts` (1 incidental `a==b; b==c`)

Conclusion: this is a local idiom, not a pervasive one. Per XNC that argues against growing core
harness surface and toward a thin helper.

## Baseline: no native primitive

- JavaScript: `===` and `Object.is` are strictly binary; `node:assert` ships only binary equality
  asserts. Idiomatic "all equal" expressions (`arr.every(x => x === arr[0])`, `new Set(arr).size === 1`)
  are boolean expressions, not assertions, so they give no diagnostic on failure.
- Our harness (`@monochromatic-dev/module-test`): the whole `MatcherSet` is binary (`toBe` = chai
  `.equal`/`===`, `toEqual`/`toStrictEqual` = deep). No N-ary matcher.

## Prior-art flavors surveyed

Every mainstream library expresses "all equal" the same way: apply an `equals(anchor)` matcher to
every element via an each/all combinator. None ships a dedicated "these N values are mutually equal"
primitive.

- RSpec `all` (Ruby, built-in): `expect([1,3,5]).to all(be_odd)`; anchored: `all(eq(roots.first))`.
- chai-each (JS chai plugin): `.each` chains standard assertions, `expect(roots).to.each.equal(first)`.
- jest-extended `toSatisfyAll` (JS Jest plugin): `expect(roots).toSatisfyAll(r => r === first)`.
- Java Hamcrest `everyItem(equalTo(v))`.
- PyHamcrest `only_contains(v)` (non-matcher args auto-wrapped in `equal_to`).
- python-precisely `all_elements(equal_to(42))`.
- AssertJ `containsOnly(v)` / `allSatisfy(pred)`; inverse `doesNotHaveDuplicates` is a named primitive.

Two sub-shapes, both anchored: value-anchored (every element equals a known value) and
predicate/matcher-anchored (every element satisfies a matcher). None offers a zero-config mutual
equality with no anchor; the `find*Root` case has no external expected value, so you anchor on `arr[0]`.

## Vetting: is any of these adoptable as a dependency?

No. Findings:

- chai-each (`jamesthomasonjr/chai-each`): DISQUALIFIED. npm stuck at v0.0.1, last commit 2018-11-05,
  no release in ~6 years. Two open bugs untouched for 5-6 years, one a core correctness defect
  ("Only the last array element is being checked", open since 2019). Mechanism monkeypatches
  `chai.Assertion.prototype` globally (overwrites every method behind an `each` flag). And it cannot
  reach our public API regardless: our `expect(x)` returns a fixed `MatcherSet` facade, never chai's
  Assertion, so `.each` would be unreachable without us writing wrapper plumbing anyway.
- jest-extended: actively maintained (v7, 2025), but registers matchers through Jest's `expect.extend`
  API. Our harness is a hand-rolled chai-backed `expect` with no `expect.extend` equivalent. Not
  plumbable without reimplementing it ourselves.
- RSpec / Java Hamcrest / PyHamcrest / python-precisely: cross-language, not JS. Reference flavors only.

Net: there is no third-party dependency to adopt. The decision is purely which API flavor to hand-roll
into our own harness or as a local helper.

## Candidate flavors to hand-roll

- A. Array-actual matcher, mutual, anchor-on-first internally: `expect([a,b,c]).toAllBe()`
  (strict, mirrors `toBe`); optional `toAllEqual()` (deep, mirrors `toEqual`). Reads well, parallels
  existing names, but adds matcher surface (auto-wrapped into `.not`/`.rejects`/`.resolves` + scoped
  counter, needs `Array.isArray` guard + `<2` misuse throw, plus PKG/TCV tests + README).
- B. Predicate matcher (jest-extended flavor): `expect([a,b,c]).toSatisfyAll(r => r === first)`.
  General, but for equality you hand-write the predicate and lose chai's value diff on failure.
- C. Composable each + matcher (RSpec/chai-each flavor): `expect([a,b,c]).each.toBe(first)`. Cleanest
  conceptually, but our `MatcherSet` is flat, not composable; exposing `.each` is a real architectural
  change to the facade.
- D. Free helper, anchor-on-first (no new matcher): `expectAllToBe([a,b,c])`. Three lines, zero facade
  surface, keeps chai's precise per-pair diff. Matches the measured-local prevalence.

```ts
function expectAllToBe(values: readonly unknown[],): void {
  const [first, ...rest,] = values;
  for (const value of rest) {
    expect(value,).toBe(first,);
  }
}
```

## Open decisions (need input)

1. Real dependency vs hand-roll: vetting says no adoptable dependency, so hand-roll. (Confirm.)
2. Placement: local test helper in `fs-path` vs shared harness API in `module-test`.
3. Flavor: D (helper) vs A (matcher) vs B/C.
4. Equality scope: strict only (`toBe`) vs also deep (`toEqual`).

## Leaning

D (local `expectAllToBe` helper, strict, anchor-on-first), promoted to a `module-test` export only if a
second use site outside `fs-path` appears. Rationale: prevalence is local (3 files), prior art shows the
proven shape is "every element equals the anchor", and a helper delivers that with no facade cost while
preserving chai's per-pair failure diff.

## Status: approved (2026-06-10)

Resolved via a grilling session; see the resolution comment below for the decided design. The original A/B/C framing in the plan doc is superseded. Implementation has not started.

## Plan document

See `docs/migration/mise-nushell-to-node.md` (committed locally as `f82d872d`, pending push to the remote).

## Summary

We are migrating the repo's primary runtime to Node. This issue tracks the question of whether to set mise's task shell to Node and migrate every task body off nushell.

Key constraint, verified on Node `v26.3.0`: an inline shell of `node -e` evaluates the body as JavaScript. It handles TS type stripping, ESM imports, top-level await, and fail-fast cleanly, but a plain command line such as `cargo build --release` is not valid JS and would have to be routed through `node:child_process`. Most of the repo's task bodies are exactly such command runners.

Measured scope: 121 `mise.toml` files, 74 with inline `run`, 263 inline bodies. Only ~8 files carry real nushell logic (root, terminal, tofu, music-player, forbidden-strings, rust); the rest are command runners.

## Decisions needed before any work starts

- Which approach: B (logic to Node-run `mise.*.ts`, command runners stay shell; recommended), A (literal `node -e` everywhere), or C (Node shell-in-JS layer such as zx). Plan ranks B > C > A.
- File-task interpreter policy: `#!/usr/bin/env node` shebang, `use_file_shell_for_executable_tasks = true`, or non-executable `.ts`.

> *This was generated by AI during triage.*

## Problem

`docs/handover/slint-app-testing.md` currently points at nested niri for live GPU/winit Slint testing.
That works, but it pulls in a full compositor and on Bazzite needed a system-wide rpm-ostree overlay.
For this repo's tests we need much less than niri.

## Goal

Build a repo-owned minimal nested Wayland session tool that launches one app and exposes the control surfaces needed by automated GUI tests.
It should replace the optional nested-niri path for Slint GPU testing.

Suggested home: `packages/cli/nested-wayland-session` as a Rust CLI, unless implementation finds a better existing package category.

## Required behavior

- Launch exactly one child app inside a nested Wayland compositor window.
  - The child receives a nested `WAYLAND_DISPLAY`.
  - The child is always maximized or fullscreen within the nested output.
  - The tool exits cleanly when the child exits.
- Screenshot current output to PNG.
- Record by periodically taking screenshots into a directory.
  - This is a PNG frame sequence, not video encoding.
  - Include configurable interval and stop condition.
- Automated input:
  - click at output coordinates;
  - key press and release;
  - text typing if feasible through the same input path.
- Resizing:
  - resizing the outer host window resizes the nested output;
  - the child stays maximized, so the app sees the new size.
- Local automation interface:
  - usable from tests and agent scripts;
  - no auth needed if bound only to a private Unix socket or loopback endpoint;
  - commands should return machine-readable success or failure.

## Non-goals

- No tiling, window management, app launcher, bars, portals, or desktop session integration.
- No multi-app support beyond rejecting or ignoring additional child windows with a clear error.
- No real video encoder in the first version.
- No dependency on niri, cage, or another external nested compositor for core operation.

## Acceptance criteria

- A mise task can run a Slint desktop app inside the nested session with GPU/winit rendering.
- A test or scripted demo launches the music-player desktop app paused, captures a PNG screenshot, injects at least one click or key event, resizes the outer window, and captures a second PNG at the new size.
- Recording mode produces a timestamped PNG sequence at the configured interval.
- `docs/handover/slint-app-testing.md` is updated to replace the nested-niri optional section with the new tool.
- `docs/troubleshooting/niri-mise-cargo-install.md` remains as historical context, but normal Slint GPU testing no longer requires installing niri.

## Implementation notes

A small Smithay or equivalent Rust compositor is likely the right shape: nested output hosted in a winit window, one toplevel child kept maximized, and a narrow control API for screenshot and input injection.
Keep the API intentionally small so this stays a test fixture, not a desktop environment.

> *This was generated by AI during triage.* ## Agent Brief **Category:** enhancement **Summary:** `git-policy/cli` re-implements its own small helpers per module: git invocation and output capture, path resolution and containment, byte-wise ordering, patch construction, option-token scanning and process liveness. They differ in the line splitter (`completeLines` versus `completePatchLines`) and in the missing-final-newline marker: a `NO_NEWLINE_MARKER` constant in one, an inline ``String.raw`\ No newline at end of file` `` in the other. `completeLines` itself exists three times (both patch builders' packages plus `final-newline-patch.ts:37-46`), and `commit-replay-patch.ts:113-138` carries a fourth, newline-preserving splitter. Byte ordering (C596, C851). Five comparators order git paths or ref names by bytes, and they disagree about encoding: - `gitOrder` in `src/policy-engine/commit-capture-order-capture.ts:192-206` encodes both sides as `latin1`. - `byteOrder` in `src/policy-engine/commit-replay.ts:137-151` encodes both as `utf8`. - `comparePathBytes` in `src/policy-engine/fix-summary.ts:48-56` uses the default `utf8`. - `comparePathBytes` in `src/policy-engine/commit-transaction-candidate-snapshot.ts:92-100` and `direct-fix-convergence.ts:292-300` also use the default. - `byteOrder` in `src/shadow-repository/shadow-refs.ts:195-209` uses an explicit `utf8`. For any path with a non-ASCII byte, `latin1` and `utf8` produce different byte sequences, so the capture-order sort and the replay sort can order the same two paths differently. Path safety (C511, C850, C660 reported with the filesystem issue). Two traversal-segment predicates with different coverage: `traversalSegment` (`src/policy-engine/commit-transaction-patch.ts:140-142`) rejects `..` and `.`, while `isUnsafeSegment` (`src/trust/registry-path.ts:213-216`) also rejects an empty segment, which is what a doubled separator produces. `absoluteGitPath` exists twice (`src/policy-engine/add-policy-facts.ts:87-98` with `cwd`, `src/policy-engine/commit-transaction-recovery-target.ts:54-67` with `effectiveCwd`), so which directory a git-reported path resolves against is decided in two places.
